questions.question: In a metric space $(\boldsymbol{X},d_{\boldsymbol{X}})$, what does it mean for $\boldsymbol{E}\subseteq\boldsymbol{X}$ to be bounded?
options: Every ball in $\boldsymbol{X}$ contains $\boldsymbol{E}$.
$\boldsymbol{E}$ contains every ball centred at each of its points.
$\boldsymbol{E}$ has no points outside the origin.
There exists $M \gt 0$ such that some ball $\boldsymbol{B}_{(\boldsymbol{X},d_{\boldsymbol{X}})}(\boldsymbol{x},M)$ contains $\boldsymbol{E}$.

questions.question: Which phrase best describes a bounded set?
options: It contains every point of the metric space.
It fits entirely inside some large enough ball.
It contains no open metric ball.
It must be a sphere.

questions.question: Which set is a bounded example in $\mathbb{R}^3$?
options: $\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2: y = x^2\}$
$\mathbb{R}^2$

questions.question: Which set is unbounded?
options: $\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2: y = x^2\}$
$\varnothing$

questions.question: Which condition is equivalent to boundedness of $\boldsymbol{E}$?
options: $\displaystyle \sup_{\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}\in\boldsymbol{E}} d_{\boldsymbol{X}}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})$ is infinite.
$\boldsymbol{E}$ contains no two distinct points.
Every point of $\boldsymbol{X}$ lies in $\boldsymbol{E}$.
$\displaystyle \sup_{\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}\in\boldsymbol{E}} d_{\boldsymbol{X}}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})$ is finite.

questions.question: What can be concluded about a subset of a bounded set?
options: It is bounded.
It is always unbounded.
It must be equal to the original set.
It must be an open ball.

questions.question: If $\boldsymbol{E}$ is bounded and $\boldsymbol{F}\subseteq\boldsymbol{E}$, what can you say about $\boldsymbol{F}$?
options: $\boldsymbol{F}$ is bounded.
$\boldsymbol{F}$ is unbounded unless it is finite.
$\boldsymbol{F}$ is bounded only if it contains the centre of the ball.
$\boldsymbol{F}$ is not a subset of any ball.

questions.question: Suppose $\displaystyle \sup_{\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}\in\boldsymbol{E}} d_{\boldsymbol{X}}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}) = 7$. Which conclusion follows?
options: $\boldsymbol{E}$ is bounded.
$\boldsymbol{E}$ is unbounded.
$\boldsymbol{E}$ must be empty.
$\boldsymbol{E}$ must be the whole metric space.

questions.question: Why does the definition allow the centre $\boldsymbol{x}$ of the containing ball to be chosen in $\boldsymbol{X}$ rather than requiring a special centre?
options: Boundedness requires $\boldsymbol{x}$ to be outside $\boldsymbol{X}$.
Boundedness requires every possible centre to work with the same radius.
Boundedness only requires that $\boldsymbol{E}$ fit inside some sufficiently large ball.
Boundedness is independent of the metric.

questions.question: Which statement correctly avoids a common misconception about boundedness?
options: A set is bounded only if it is exactly a metric ball.
A set is bounded only if it contains the origin.
A set is bounded only if every metric-space point lies in it.
A set may be bounded without being a ball itself.

questions.question: If $\boldsymbol{E}$ is the unit sphere in $\mathbb{R}^3$ and $\boldsymbol{F}$ is any subset of $\boldsymbol{E}$, which statement follows?
options: $\boldsymbol{F}$ is unbounded if it has infinitely many points.
$\boldsymbol{F}$ is bounded.
$\boldsymbol{F}$ is unbounded unless it is a sphere.
$\boldsymbol{F}$ cannot be contained in any ball.

questions.question: Which observation best shows that the parabola $\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2:y = x^2\}$ is unbounded?
options: It has no points in $\mathbb{R}^2$.
It is exactly a unit sphere.
Its pairwise distances must all be zero under the stated limiting assumptions.
Its points cannot all fit inside one sufficiently large ball.

questions.question: What does it mean for $\boldsymbol E$ to be bounded in a metric space?
options: It is contained in some ball of finite radius.
It contains every ball in the space.
It has no points.
It is always closed.

questions.question: What does the constant $M \gt 0$ represent for boundedness?
options: A radius of a ball containing the set
The number of points in the set
The dimension of the metric space
The smallest element of the set

questions.question: What is preserved when taking a subset of a bounded set?
options: Boundedness
Unboundedness
Being the whole metric space
Having no metric

questions.question: Is $\{x\in\mathbb R:|x|\le5\}$ bounded in the usual metric?
options: No, it contains infinitely many points.
Yes, it fits inside a ball of finite radius.
No, every subset of $\mathbb R$ is unbounded.
Yes, only because it is empty.

questions.question: Is $\mathbb R$ bounded in the usual metric?
options: No, no finite-radius ball contains all real numbers.
Yes, every metric space is bounded.
Yes, it is contained in $B(0,1)$.
No, because it is closed under the stated limiting assumptions.

questions.question: If $\boldsymbol E$ is bounded and $\boldsymbol F\subseteq\boldsymbol E$, what follows?
options: $\boldsymbol F$ is unbounded.
$\boldsymbol F$ is bounded.
$\boldsymbol F$ must be empty.
$\boldsymbol F$ must equal $\boldsymbol E$.

questions.question: Which finite-diameter condition is equivalent to boundedness?
options: Every pairwise distance is infinite
$\sup_{\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol y\in\boldsymbol E}d(\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol y)$ is finite
The set has exactly one point
The set contains its boundary

questions.question: Suppose $d(\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol y)\le10$ for all $\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol y\in\boldsymbol E$. What does the finite-diameter criterion imply?
options: $\boldsymbol E$ is bounded.
$\boldsymbol E$ is unbounded.
$\boldsymbol E$ is empty only.
$\boldsymbol E$ is not a subset of the metric space.
